title: Small propulsive-landing (VTVL) rockets: verified examples for ARGOS H1
units: SI (lbf and kgf quoted as published, with SI conversion)
evidence_rule: Only facts read on fetched pages; missing values marked MISSING; DERIVED values computed from published figures; ours = estimates/SIM, not physical approval.

ours.name: ARGOS H1 (engine CAD v3.5.1 in GNC reference vehicle RV-1c)
ours.status: Nothing built or flown. Engine = real CAD v3.5.1; N2O tank = concept, length ESTIMATE; airframe/fins/legs/nose/bays = ASSUMED GNC reference vehicle RV-1c (not Lauty's design); masses = current lead estimate, not frozen; flight figures = SIM.
ours.propulsion: hybrid N2O/ABS (2.0 kg N2O, 0.40 kg ABS grain), pintle throttle (throttle_frac = F/500 N), gimballed engine (8 deg stop, slew >= 100 deg/s)
ours.flight_profile_SIM: full-thrust TVC ascent -> MECO -> nose-first coast -> nose drogue at apogee -> engine relight at ~57-67 m and ~22 m/s -> throttled TVC landing burn -> touchdown ~1 m/s on 4 deployable legs (gnc.json v3.1 flight_profile.note_v3)

examples.name: Colibri
examples.builder: Gruyere Space Program (GSP), Swiss student association at EPFL
examples.propulsion: Liquid bipropellant N2O/IPA, in-house F-100 engine: 1.2 kN at launch; rated 1 kN, throttleable 25-125 %; gimballed ('orientable') engine guided by GNSS + INS. Not a hybrid.
examples.size_mass: 2.5 m tall, ~100 kg ('100-kilogram, 2.5-metre rocket hopper'; wet/dry basis not stated). Diameter MISSING.
examples.what_it_did: FREE PROPULSIVE LANDING: YES. First tested 2 Jun 2024; 22 low hops on a passive safety harness by 13 Aug 2024 (max 8 m); then a free-flight campaign of eight free flights over three days, the highest to 105 m with ~30 m lateral translation and return to the pad, ~60 s (announced 18 Oct 2024). Over 50 flights in total; described as the first rocket hopper to fly freely in Europe.
examples.comparison_to_ours: Closest published analogue found: N2O oxidiser, throttled and gimballed, 2.5 m vs our 2.03 m. But ~5.7x our liftoff mass (100 vs ~17.4 kg), 2.4x our max thrust (1.2 kN vs 500 N); DERIVED liftoff T/W ~1.2 vs our ~2.9. Liquid N2O/IPA, not hybrid. Continuous-burn hop (engine on from take-off to touchdown), not our boost-coast-drogue-relight-landing sequence. Its harnessed-hops-then-free-flight campaign is a precedent for a staged test plan.
examples.evidence_quote: "During the flight, Colibri took off and flew to an altitude of 105 meters. It then flew 30 meters southeast before returning to the launchpad and performing a successful landing." (Interesting Engineering, 22 Oct 2024) | "Colibri is the first rocket hopper to fly freely in Europe" (JAVAD customer story)

examples.name: Scout F
examples.propulsion: Hobby solid motors (designations MISSING): ascent motor, then a separately ignited descent (landing) motor. Servo-driven TVC mount (3D-printed, later machined aluminium). No throttle: thrust shaped by 'a pair of ceramic pincers which block the thrust of the motors as required'. Carbon-fibre spring legs released by nichrome wire.
examples.size_mass: MISSING (not stated on any fetched page; model-rocket scale).
examples.what_it_did: FREE PROPULSIVE LANDING: YES (launched model rocket landing on its own descent motor and legs; no tether in any source). Reported 1-5 Aug 2022 after seven years of attempts begun in 2015. Altitude and landing accuracy MISSING.
examples.comparison_to_ours: Closest in mission profile: TVC ascent, unpowered coast, then a separate landing burn on deployable legs, like our boost-coast-relight-landing. Differs in propulsion (unthrottleable solid motors vs our throttled hybrid relight) and scale (hobby motors; mass MISSING, certainly not comparable to 17.4 kg or 500 N on the evidence available).
examples.evidence_quote: "Now, 7 years into the rollercoaster journey, he has finally achieved that goal with the latest version of his Scout rocket." (Hackaday, 5 Aug 2022) | "The rocket is notable for being, by all accounts I could find, the first model rocket landed with solid rocket motors." (The Drive, 2 Aug 2022)

examples.name: Xombie (XA-0.1B)
examples.builder: Masten Space Systems (small company, Mojave, USA)
examples.propulsion: Liquid LOX/isopropyl alcohol, single regeneratively cooled engine: 750 lbf design (3.3 kN, spring 2009), over 810 lbf (3.6 kN) in Sep 2009, ~900 lbf (~4 kN) by Oct 2009 per Wikipedia. Throttle and gimbal details MISSING on fetched pages.
examples.size_mass: MISSING (no height or mass for XA-0.1B on any fetched page).
examples.what_it_did: FREE PROPULSIVE LANDING: YES. Crane-tethered hops from May 2009; first free flight 19 Sep 2009; longest flight 93 s between two pads 60 m apart, landing 'within a few inches of the target'. Won the NASA Lunar Lander Challenge Level One second prize (USD 150,000) on 7 Oct 2009 with 16 cm average landing accuracy.
examples.comparison_to_ours: Small-company precedent for the crane-tether-then-free-flight path and for precision pad landings. ~6.7-8x our max thrust (3.3-4.0 kN vs 500 N); mass MISSING. Cryogenic liquid bipropellant, continuous-burn hops, not a hybrid and no coast/relight.
examples.evidence_quote: "The longest flight spanned 93 seconds and took place between two pads 60 meters apart" ... "We landed within a few inches of the target." (Military & Aerospace Electronics, 23 Sep 2009) | "XA-0.1B, nicknamed "Xombie", first flew free of tether 19 September 2009" (Wikipedia)

examples.name: Gyroc
examples.builder: Airborne Engineering Ltd (AEL), Westcott, UK (small company)
examples.propulsion: Liquid N2O/IPA, two propellant tanks; custom gimballed engine with custom control actuators; actuated throttling valves. Thrust MISSING.
examples.what_it_did: FREE PROPULSIVE LANDING: NO (tethered). First flown 2019. June 2019 test: took off from blocks, hovered briefly with only the attitude and altitude loops closed (no sideways control), descended and shut down, tethered to a gantry. AEL states it 'can hover for over 30 seconds' (capability, no dated result). Later in an ESA programme. No free flight or landing on legs reported.
examples.comparison_to_ours: Nearest in mass found (~20 kg vs our ~17.4 kg estimate) and same oxidiser, throttled and gimballed. But liquid N2O/IPA (not hybrid), thrust MISSING, and only tethered hovers published: it does not demonstrate a free landing.
examples.evidence_quote: "It is tethered to a gantry to prevent damage to the vehicle in the event that it has to be shut down prematurely." (AEL news, 13 Jun 2019)

examples.name: HTTP-3AT (tethered hover testbed; successor HTTP-4)
examples.builder: Advanced Rocket Research Center (ARRC), Hsinchu, Taiwan (university-based research centre)
examples.propulsion: Hybrid ('hybrid rocket boosters'): four Sam-a-Tsiau engines, the HTTP-3A second-stage engine, with four main throttle valves and TVC actuators. Propellants MISSING. ARRC lists 150 kgf x 4 vacuum thrust for the HTTP-3A second stage, not confirmed for the 3AT at sea level.
examples.size_mass: MISSING (no dimensions or mass on fetched pages).
examples.what_it_did: FREE PROPULSIVE LANDING: NO (tethered; the 'T' stands for Tethered). 2020 tethered hover series: crash on the 3rd attempt (no explosion), first successful hover of 1 s on the 5th (20 Aug 2020), 25 s hover on the 6th (8 Sep 2020). ARRC claims 'first in the world to achieve VTVL with hybrid rockets' (self-claim, tethered, not independently verified). Successor HTTP-4: hybrid VTVL vehicle with one gimballed engine driven by two direct-drive servos, a throttle valve, a blow-down oxidiser tank and cold-gas roll verniers. Its test dates, tether status and landing outcome are MISSING.
examples.comparison_to_ours: The only hybrid VTVL vehicle found, the same propulsion class as our N2O/ABS hybrid. The HTTP-4 architecture (single gimballed hybrid engine, two actuators, throttle valve, blow-down oxidiser, roll provision) mirrors ours most closely. The published record shows only tethered hovers (1 s, then 25 s) and a crash: no public free hybrid landing was found. Scale MISSING.
examples.evidence_quote: "We successfully hovered in air for one second." ... "Though the HTTP-3AT rocket crashed during the third test, since we implement hybrid rocket boosters, no explosion occurred." (ARRC, 20 Aug 2020) | ARRC post on vocus.cc: "2020年9月8日,第6次繫留懸浮飛行測試,飛行測試25秒成功!" (8 Sep 2020, 6th tethered hover flight test, 25 s flight test successful)

notes: FREE (untethered) propulsive landings verified: Colibri (2024), Scout F (2022), Masten Xombie (2009). Tethered only: AEL Gyroc (2019), ARRC HTTP-3AT (2020).

No example matches our full combination: hybrid, throttled, gimballed, boost-coast-drogue-relight-landing, free landing. Scout F is the only one with a separate landing burn after a coast (solid motors). The hoppers burn continuously. The only hybrid example is tethered. This search was not exhaustive, so no originality or superiority claim follows.

DERIVED from published values: thrust-to-weight Colibri ~1.2 (1.2 kN / 100 kg; mass basis unstated) vs ours ~2.9 (500 N / 17.4 kg lead estimate). Our values are estimates/SIM only: no physical approval.

Verified but excluded as out of scale (large company): Honda experimental reusable rocket, 17 Jun 2025, Taiki (Hokkaido): 6.3 m, 0.85 m diameter, 900 kg dry / 1,312 kg wet (~75x our liftoff mass), 271.4 m altitude, 56.6 s flight, landed within 37 cm of target (https://global.honda/en/topics/2025/c_2025-06-17ceng.html). The page does not state the propellants or explicitly say 'untethered'.

Checked, NOT counted (no flight or landing found): Purdue PSP Active Controls TADPOLE (throttleable liquid engine, hot fire only; won the Collegiate Propulsive Lander Challenge Throttle Milestone, USD 15k); Space Team Aachen Hopper (N2O/ethanol, ~5 m, 180 kg wet, first hot fire 'in preparation' Jan 2026); TUM ASCENT hopper (no results published); UConn AIAA Propulsive Landing (unpowered tower drop test, Apr 2023); Konkuk Univ. hybrid VTVL (simulation only, JMST 2020); IIT Madras hybrid soft landing (hardware-in-the-loop only, 2024). Copenhagen Suborbitals: no propulsive-landing vehicle found in one search; not included.

Sources not readable: the BPS.space YouTube video page (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SH3lR2GLgT0) was refused by the WebFetch proxy with HTTP 429 (rate limited; not retried, as instructed). The Vice article on Scout F was blocked by robots.txt. So Scout F rests on secondary press (Hackaday, The Drive) and its size, mass and motor designations are MISSING.

Verification method: shell downloads were refused by the proxy (403 CONNECT), so the quotes were checked by repeat WebFetch exact-string queries on the extracted page text, not against raw HTML. The Scout F Drive quote drops the italics on 'solid'.

Source spread: Masten thrust differs by date and source: 750 lbf design, >810 lbf (Sep 2009), ~850 lbf (Technology Review, Oct 2009), ~900 lbf (Wikipedia, Oct 2009). Colibri: 1.2 kN at launch (press) vs 1 kN rated, 25-125 % (JAVAD). Colibri flight count: over 50 (JAVAD) vs 53 (Kistler).
Contradiction preserved: the brief's first-flight target apogee is 210 m (SIM), while gnc.json v3.1 flight_profile lists the A1 target as 285 m (rev2). Not reconciled here.

Carried from the brief, not researched here: the GNC v3d tank at z 0.55-0.995 m clashes with the v3.5.1 engine top at z 0.558 m. The tank moves to z 0.58-1.08 m (tank-line route TO-DEFINE), and avionics, battery and backup chute shift forward (they still fit in the 1.70 m tube).
